text.p: Germany accused the Church of Scientology on Friday of insulting millions of Jewish victims of the Nazi Holocaust.
A Foreign Ministry spokesman said the organisation had levelled "totally absurd" charges that Bonn used Nazi-style tactics against its followers, as Hitler persecuted the Jews.

But officials said they would not dignify an anti-German Scientology campaign, which kicked off with a scathing full-page advertisement in the New York Times on Thursday, by launching a formal complaint against it.
The advertisement, headlined "Practising Religious Intolerance" and "Germany Then and Now", bore the eagle and swastika insignia of Hitler's Third Reich.

The controversial ad, comparing German attitudes to the organisation with Nazi anti-Jewish persecution, also drew fire on Thursday from the U.S. State Department, which has sometimes backed Scientology's grievances against German authorities.

"This is an outrageous charge against the German government by an American group. It bears no resemblance to the facts of what's going on there," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said. "The language used is needlessly provocative."
"We believe Scientology's accusations are totally absurd," German Foreign Ministry spokesman Martin Erdmann told Reuters.

"By comparing its treatment in Germany with Nazi crimes against the Jews, Scientology is falsifying history. What is worse, it's also insulting the feelings of the victims of the Nazi regime and their relatives."
In Germany, Scientology is not classed as a church and many politicians want it placed under surveillance, accusing it of exploiting the weak for economic gain.
The advertisement described Germany as the only country systematically discriminating against Scientologists.
"You may wonder why German officials discriminate against Scientologists," it said. "There is no legitimate reason but then there was none that justified the persecution of the Jewish people either."
The regional state of Bavaria, which has been outspoken its criticism of Scientology, reacted furiously to those comments.
"This advertisment is a brutal trivialisation of the crimes against the Jews," Guenther Beckstein, the southern state's interior minister, told RTL television.
Beckstein said he had already spoken with Ignatz Bubis, the leader of Germany's Jewish community, who had pledged to ask American Jewish organisations to campaign against the ad.
Erdmann said the German government would not lodge a formal complaint about the advertisement or demand a right to reply as it believed this could add credibility to the accusations.
"We will not contribute to this campaign by taking it seriously," he said.
His restrained reaction was backed by Peter Hausmann, the government's chief spokesman.
"I've heard about the accusations and I don't find their form or their content acceptable and I won't comment any further than that," Hausmann told reporters.

Scientology was founded in 1954 by the American science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard. Would-be members take personality tests and are then offered courses and literature to help them realise what the church sees as their full potential.
Some German officials have demanded Scientology be banned or at least be observed by Bonn's anti-extremist agency, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution.

The youth wing of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) called earlier this year for a boycott of the Hollywood blockbuster "Mission:Impossible" because it stars Tom Cruise -- one of several high-profile Scientologists.
Fellow film stars Nicole Kidman, who is also Cruise's wife, and John Travolta are also members of the church.
